name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so the problem is at least partly that nothing learns. Two things could explain it. (1) The default recipe gives only about 32 PPO updates in 131k steps, with the learning rate decaying linearly to zero, which may be too few. (2) To score a placement, the network has to find the landing layer (the maximum build height under the footprint) and then check that the target is missing at that layer across the footprint. The starting network mixes all layers together in a 1x1 stem and never looks at layers separately, so this is hard for it to learn. This round tests both explanations as a 2x2 design missing one cell: a new per-layer architecture with the default recipe, the starting architecture with more and smaller updates, and the two changes together. Comparing them should show whether the architecture, the recipe or both matter. Any score above about 2-3% would be a real signal here.

### Round 2
Every trial so far scored 0, on dev and also in the last 10% of training, where actions are sampled. Neither the per-layer logsumexp head nor a recipe with more updates changed this, so none of the round-1 trials gave a signal. With about 130k steps the agent sees only about 4,000 episodes of up to 33 placements. The +1 bonus for an exact build comes only at the episode's end and is heavily discounted at gamma 0.95. My main guess is that the agent needs more samples and a longer effective horizon. Under the budget formula, 1 PPO epoch gives about 3.25 times as many environment steps (about 426k) and 2 epochs about 1.9 times. This round tests that: the baseline network at 1 epoch, the baseline at 2 epochs, and the per-layer network at 1 epoch, all with gamma 0.99. If all three stay at 0, a quirk of this world is the likely cause, and next round should change the network more.

### Round 3
Six trials have all scored 0.000, on both dev and late training success. That covers two architectures, the default recipe, more and smaller updates, 1 or 2 epochs, gamma 0.99 and up to 405k steps. Neither more samples nor the per-layer bias produced a single exact build. So the bottleneck may be something none of these covered. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. Every network so far hard-codes the action layout in its footprint pooling: top-left anchor, (dy, dx) order, which footprint belongs to which type. If the real convention differs, those heads would be wired to the wrong cells. This round drops the fixed footprint pooling in favour of learned 3x3 output convolutions, which can learn any anchor offset. It also feeds the mask's per-type legality planes and coordinate channels in as inputs, since the mask shows the real footprints at the grid edges. It also uses a lower gamma (0.9) and less entropy, because the per-step reward is dense. One candidate isolates the mask input on the baseline, and one tests global attention.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored 0 on dev and also 0 on training success. That held across recipes (1 to 4 epochs, gamma 0.9 to 0.99, 98k to 405k steps) and across architectures (footprint-pooling head, per-layer logsumexp, conv head with mask inputs, transformer). Seed noise cannot explain this. Even the easy designs with no overhangs, which a greedy 1x1 policy could build, were never built exactly, even with exploration during training. Something structural is wrong. Since the world "may not behave as described", the most likely cause is that action indices do not map to grid cells as the spec states. The axes might be transposed or flipped, the anchor might differ, or DONE might sit at a different index. Every head so far assumed spatial alignment between feature cells and action indices; a 3x3 conv can absorb a one-cell shift but not a transpose. Final round: dense action heads that learn any index-to-cell mapping, including where DONE is.
